2103463 การถ่ายเทความร้อน · Midterm covers periods 1–13 · Incropera ch. 1–5

Everything is one equation:
flow = difference ÷ resistance

If the lectures did not land, that is normal — heat transfer looks like twenty unrelated formulas. It is not. It is one idea (energy is conserved), one rate law per mode, and then a lot of bookkeeping about geometry. This page rebuilds the whole midterm from zero, in the order your syllabus teaches it, with a working example and a self-test at every step.

00

How to use this pageวิธีใช้หน้านี้

Read once · 6 minThen never again

Reading and highlighting feel productive and are among the least effective study techniques measured; practice testing and spaced practice are the two rated "high utility" in the big review by Dunlosky and colleagues.¹ So this page is built to be used, not read.

Tactic 01

Predict before you open

Every worked example is collapsed. Read the problem, guess the method and roughly the answer, then open the solution. The wrong guess is what makes the right one stick.

Tactic 02

Worked example → twin problem

Novices learn faster studying a full solution than fighting a blank page — the worked-example effect.² Each solution is followed by a Check question that changes one thing.

Tactic 03

Play the sliders

Nine interactive labs on this page. Before dragging, say out loud which way the curve will move. Physics you can predict is physics you own.

Tactic 04

Explain to the wall

Close the page and say the section title, then explain it in your own words for 60 seconds. The gaps you hear are exactly what to reread.

Tactic 05

Interleave, don't block

Do not do ten fin problems in a row. Mix a fin, a transient, a resistance problem. Harder now, far better on the exam.

Tactic 06

Bookmark and come back

Bottom-right corner: save your spot, close the tab, reopen tomorrow and jump straight back. Spacing beats cramming.

A 5-day plan that actually fits

Day 1 — §01–03. Get the vocabulary and the heat equation. Day 2 — §04–06. Resistance networks until they are automatic. Day 3 — §07 fins + redo two Day-1 checks from memory. Day 4 — §08–09, 2-D. Day 5 — §10–11 transient, then §12 method chooser as a timed drill.

Each day: 45 min learn, 10 min break, 25 min closed-book retrieval of the previous day.

How this page maps onto your slide decks

Every section header carries the syllabus periods and the Incropera sections it covers, so you can read a deck and this page side by side.

1a, 1b → §01–02  ·  2 → §03  ·  3a → §04–05  ·  3b → §06  ·  3c → §07  ·  4a → §08  ·  4b → §09  ·  5a → §10  ·  5b → §11. Sections 12–13 are exam kit, not lecture material.

01

The three modes of heat transferรูปแบบการถ่ายเทความร้อน

Periods 1–2Incropera §1.1–1.2Slides Chapter 1a

Heat transfer is thermal energy in transit because of a temperature difference. That is the whole subject. Thermodynamics told you how much energy moves between two equilibrium states; heat transfer tells you how fast, and what the temperature field looks like while it happens.

Three words your lecturer will not let you mix up
  • Thermal energy (พลังงานความร้อน) — in J, stored inside matter. A property.
  • Temperature (อุณหภูมิ) — in K or °C, an indirect measure of how much is stored.
  • Heat / heat transfer (ความร้อน / การถ่ายเทความร้อน) — in J, energy crossing a boundary. Not stored. A body does not "contain heat".
QuantitySymbolUnitsMeaning
HeatQJThermal energy transferred over a time interval
Heat rateqWEnergy transfer per unit time
Heat fluxq″W/m²Per unit time and per unit area,
Heat rate per lengthq′W/mUsed for pipes and long fins,

Conduction — การนำความร้อน

Energy handed from more energetic particles to their less energetic neighbours, by molecular vibration and (in metals) by free electrons. It needs a medium and it needs a temperature gradient. The rate law is Fourier's law:

Fourier's law · vector form
k thermal conductivity, W/m·K  ·  ∇T temperature gradient, K/m  ·  the minus sign is physics, not bookkeeping: heat flows down the temperature hill, so a negative gradient gives a positive flux.

For the simplest case — steady state, one dimension, constant , a plane wall of thickness — the temperature profile is a straight line and the flux is constant:

Convection — การพาความร้อน

Conduction at the wall plus bulk motion of a fluid sweeping the energy away. All of that messy fluid mechanics is buried in one coefficient , and the rate law is deliberately trivial:

Newton's law of cooling
h convection coefficient, W/m²·K — not a property of the fluid. It depends on geometry, velocity, fluid properties and even on . Finding is the entire second half of your course.

Forced convection (การพาแบบบังคับ): flow driven by a fan or pump. Free / natural convection (การพาแบบอิสระ): flow driven by buoyancy alone. Same equation, wildly different : free convection in air is roughly 2–25 W/m²·K, forced air 25–250, water 50–20 000, boiling and condensation 2 500–100 000.

Radiation — การแผ่รังสีความร้อน

Every surface above absolute zero emits electromagnetic waves. No medium required — this is how the Sun reaches you. Emission from a real surface:

Emission, absorption, and net exchange with large surroundings
ε emissivity,  ·  σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴  ·  the last form assumes a small surface inside large surroundings at and a grey surface ().
The single most common exam mistake in Chapter 1

must be in kelvin. Always. A difference like is identical in °C and K, so convection forgives you. does not. 200 °C is 473 K, and is nowhere near .

To put radiation into a resistance network alongside convection, linearise it into a radiation heat transfer coefficient:

Then combined surface loss is simply , and if you may add .

Example 1Steam pipe losing heat two ways  HIGH YIELD

An uninsulated steam pipe passes through a room. The pipe outer diameter is mm and its surface is at °C with emissivity . The room air and the walls are both at 25 °C, and the convection coefficient on the pipe is W/m²·K. Find the heat loss per unit length of pipe.

Known: D = 0.07 m, T_s = 200 °C = 473 K, T_∞ = T_sur = 25 °C = 298 K h = 15 W/m²·K, ε = 0.8, σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴ Assume: steady state; large surroundings; grey surface (α = ε)
SolutionOpen only after you have tried it
  1. Set up the surface energy balance. The surface loses heat by convection and by radiation, in parallel:
  2. Convection term. Note °C is fine here — it is a difference.
  3. Radiation term — kelvin only.
  4. Add them. W/m.
  5. Sanity check. The equivalent radiation coefficient is which is comparable to . Radiation is not a small correction here — it is 42 % of the loss.
Answer W per metre of pipe  (577 W/m convection + 421 W/m radiation)
CheckSame pipe, but someone points a fan at it and h rises to 100 W/m²·K. What fraction of the loss is now radiation?

Radiation is unchanged at 421 W/m because it depends only on , and . Convection becomes W/m. Total 4269 W/m, so radiation is 9.9 %.

The lesson: whether radiation "matters" is never a property of the surface alone — it is a comparison of against . Compute first, then decide.

02

Conservation of energyการอนุรักษ์พลังงาน

Period 2Incropera §1.3Slides Chapter 1b

This is the tool that turns "here are three rate laws" into "here is the temperature". Draw a dashed control surface, label every arrow crossing it, and write:

Control volume · at an instant
in / out surface phenomena — conduction, convection, radiation, flow work  ·  g generation, a volumetric conversion from electrical/nuclear/chemical energy  ·  st storage, the rate of change of energy inside.

The special case you will use constantly: the surface energy balance

Shrink the control volume onto the surface itself. It now has zero volume and zero mass, so generation and storage vanish — even if the material behind the surface is generating heat or heating up:

Surface energy balance · valid steady AND transient
Why this matters more than it looks

The surface balance is what couples the solid to the fluid. Inside the solid you solve the heat equation; the surface balance is the boundary condition that tells that solution what the outside world is doing. Almost every problem in Chapters 3 and 5 is: solve inside, then match at the surface.

Example 2A chip that must not exceed 85 °C

A square silicon chip 12.5 mm × 12.5 mm dissipates W. Its back is bonded to a substrate through which W is conducted away; the top face is cooled by air at °C with W/m²·K. Radiation is negligible. Is the chip below its 85 °C limit at steady state?

SolutionTry it first — draw the control surface
  1. Control volume = the chip. Steady state so . Electrical dissipation is generation:
  2. Solve for convection. W.
  3. Apply Newton's law of cooling on the top face. m².
  4. °C.
Answer≈ 294 °C — the chip fails catastrophically. Air at cannot remove 4.2 W from 1.6 cm². You need a heat sink, i.e. fins — which is exactly why §07 exists.

Reverse the question the way an exam would: what keeps at 85 °C? W/m²·K — impossible in air, easy in a liquid coolant.

03

Fourier's law and the heat diffusion equationสมการการนำความร้อน

Periods 3–4Incropera ch. 2Slides Chapter 2

Chapter 1 gave rate laws. Chapter 2 gives the differential equation whose solution is the temperature field . Once you have , Fourier's law hands you the flux anywhere, any time. That two-step is the entire methodology of the course:

The methodology, memorise it

1. Write the correct simplified form of the heat equation. 2. Integrate it, applying boundary and initial conditions, to get . 3. Differentiate and use Fourier's law to get , then multiply by area for .

Where the heat equation comes from

Take a differential box , write , expand each outflow as a Taylor series , then substitute Fourier's law. Everything cancels except:

Heat diffusion equation · Cartesian, general
Left three terms: net conduction in. Fourth: generation in W/m³. Right: storage. Read it as an energy balance, not as calculus.

If is constant, divide through by :

What α actually means — สภาพแพร่ความร้อน

Thermal diffusivity is the ratio of how well a material conducts energy to how much energy it must store to change temperature. Large (copper, m²/s) = responds to thermal changes fast. Small (brick, ) = sluggish. It controls every transient problem in Chapter 5; alone controls every steady one in Chapters 3–4.

The same equation in radial coordinates

Cylindrical
Spherical
You will never be asked to derive these. You will be asked to cross out the terms that vanish and integrate what is left. That is the actual skill.

Boundary and initial conditions — เงื่อนไขขอบเขต

The heat equation is second order in space (so two boundary conditions per direction) and first order in time (so one initial condition). There are only three kinds of boundary condition in this course:

  1. The curvature is the clue. With no generation, steady 1-D constant- conduction gives — a straight line. This profile is curved, so .
  2. Differentiate and apply Fourier's law. , so
  3. At : W. Positive: heat flows in the direction, i.e. into the wall.
  4. At : °C/m, so W.
  5. More comes out than went in — the extra 180 W must be generated inside. Use the heat equation :
  6. Cross-check by energy balance. W . ✓
Answer W in, W out, W/m³
CheckWithout any numbers: what shape is T(x) in a plane wall, a cylindrical shell, and a spherical shell — all steady, no generation, constant k?

Plane wall: ⟹ linear in .
Cylindrical shell: ⟹ logarithmic, .

And the reason is always the same: the rate must be constant with radius (steady, no generation), but the area grows, so the flux must fall — which forces the gradient to flatten as increases. This one question is a favourite; Assignment II asks it as questions 1–2.

04

Plane wall & the thermal resistance networkผนังระนาบและความต้านทานความร้อน

Period 5Incropera §3.1–3.4Slides Chapter 3a

This is the single highest-value section of the midterm. Get the resistance analogy into your fingers and a third of the exam becomes bookkeeping.

Solve the heat equation for a plane wall — steady, 1-D, no generation, constant — and you get , so is linear and

Rewrite that last equation as difference over resistance and the entire chapter opens up:

The analogy that runs the whole course
Voltage → temperature difference · current → heat rate · electrical resistance → thermal resistance. Series resistances add. Parallel resistances combine as reciprocals. Everything you know from circuits transfers unchanged.
Composite wall · the workhorse formula
And to get any intermediate temperature, apply the same rule to a partial network: . Never re-derive; just walk the circuit.

Overall heat transfer coefficient — สัมประสิทธิ์การถ่ายเทความร้อนรวม

U [W/m²·K] is just Newton's law of cooling stretched across the whole assembly. For a plane wall is unambiguous. For a tube it is not — see §05.

Thermal contact resistance — ความต้านทานที่ผิวสัมผัส

Two solids pressed together do not touch everywhere. Real contact happens at a few asperity peaks; between them sit gas-filled gaps. That extra drop is:

Bigger when: rougher surfaces, lower contact pressure, a low-conductivity interstitial gas. Smaller when you raise pressure, use a soft interface metal or thermal grease, or replace air with helium. Evacuating the gap increases resistance — the gas was helping.

Example 4How much insulation to lose only 100 W?  SLIDE EXAMPLE 3.1

A person's skin/fat layer is 3 mm thick with W/m·K over a body surface area m². Inner body temperature is °C. The person wears an insulating layer of W/m·K and stands in air at °C with W/m²·K and a radiation coefficient W/m²·K acting in parallel. What insulation thickness limits the heat loss to 100 W, and what is the skin temperature? Repeat for water at 10 °C with W/m²·K and no radiation.

SolutionDraw the circuit before you touch a number
  1. The circuit. Skin/fat in series with insulation in series with (convection ∥ radiation): Convection and radiation are parallel because both act on the same surface between the same two temperatures — so their conductances add, .
  2. Required total resistance. The whole point of "limit the loss to 100 W" is that it fixes before you know any geometry:
  3. Solve for the thickness. Air case, :
  4. Water case, , no radiation: More insulation is needed in water because the fluid-side resistance you were getting for free has essentially vanished.
  5. Skin temperature — walk only the first resistor:
Answer4.4 mm in air, 6.1 mm in water, °C in both cases
Why is Ts the same in both?

Because depends only on , and the skin/fat resistance — none of which changed. Everything downstream of that resistor is irrelevant to it. Reading the circuit tells you this before any algebra.

CheckAssignment II Q7: if h₀ = 5h᎐, which surface temperature sits closer to its adjoining fluid?

The same passes through both convection resistances, so . With , the outer resistance is five times smaller, so is five times smaller than .

The outer surface hugs the outside air; the inner surface sits well away from the inside air. General rule to memorise: small resistance ⇒ small temperature drop. A surface with a huge is essentially at the fluid temperature.

05

Cylinders, spheres, and the critical radiusทรงกระบอกและทรงกลม · รัศมีวิกฤต

Period 6Incropera §3.3Slides Chapter 3a

Everything from §04 carries over. Only one thing changes, and it changes everything: the area through which heat passes is no longer constant. It grows as in a cylinder and in a sphere.

The one sentence that explains all of §05

At steady state with no generation, the heat rate is the same through every radius (it has nowhere else to go), but the area grows with . Therefore the flux must fall as increases, and so the temperature gradient flattens outward. That is why is logarithmic in a cylinder and -shaped in a sphere instead of straight.

Trap: U for a tube is meaningless without naming a surface

is always a constant, but alone is not — . If a problem gives you for a tube, it must also say which area (inner or outer) it refers to. .

Critical radius of insulation — รัศมีวิกฤตของฉนวน

Add insulation to a pipe and two things happen at once, pulling in opposite directions: conduction resistance rises (thicker layer), but convection resistance falls (larger outer area). For a bare cylinder with insulation of conductivity and outer radius :

Set :

Critical radius
The second derivative at is , so this stationary point is a minimum of resistance = maximum of heat loss. There is no "optimum insulation thickness" — you want to be on the far side of , or not near it at all.
How to answer the exam version of this

Compute and compare to the bare pipe radius . If — the usual case for real pipes — any insulation you add reduces the loss immediately. If — thin wires, small tubes — the first millimetres of insulation increase the loss. That is exactly why electrical wire insulation helps a wire run cooler.

Example 6Generating wall A bonded to a plain wall B  SLIDE EXAMPLE 3.7

Wall A ( mm, W/m·K) generates uniformly at W/m³. Its left face is perfectly insulated. Its right face is bonded to wall B ( mm, W/m·K), whose outer face is cooled by a fluid at °C with W/m²·K. Contact resistance is negligible. Sketch and find the two surface temperatures (A–B interface) and (outer face of B).

SolutionHint: start with the flux, not the temperature
  1. Where does the heat go? The left face is insulated, so all the generated energy must exit to the right. Energy balance on wall A per unit area: This one number now drives everything downstream.
  2. Wall B has no generation, so from here on the resistance concept is legal again:
  3. Outer face — one resistor from the fluid:
  4. Interface — two resistors from the fluid:
  5. Peak temperature, at the insulated face of A. The insulated face behaves exactly like the mid-plane of a symmetric wall of half-thickness , so use the parabola with :
  6. The sketch. In A: a downward-opening parabola, flat (zero slope) at the insulated face, steepening toward the interface. In B: a straight line, since . Then a jump-free but sloped drop across the convection film to 30 °C.
Answer °C, °C, peak °C
CheckAssignment II Q13: can a generating solid with a perfectly insulated surface ever reach steady state?

No. Steady state requires , i.e. . With a perfectly insulated surface and , leaving . Energy accumulates forever and the temperature rises without bound.

And Q14: a wall of thickness with identical convection on both faces is identical to a wall of thickness with one face insulated — because symmetry makes the mid-plane adiabatic. Same equation, same answer, half the work. Recognising this saves you minutes in an exam.

07

Fins — heat transfer from extended surfacesครีบระบายความร้อน

Periods 7–8Incropera §3.6, Table 3.4Slides Chapter 3cAssignment II Q15–21

Newton's law says . To raise you can raise (expensive: bigger fan, different fluid) or raise — for free, by growing metal out of the surface. That is a fin.

But a fin is not free area. Heat has to conduct along the fin before it can convect off, so the fin tip is cooler than its base and the extra area is not working at full . The whole of §07 is quantifying that penalty.

Your slides give the formal definition: an extended surface is a solid in which conduction is assumed one-dimensional, while heat is simultaneously convected (and/or radiated) from the surface in the transverse direction. Two directions at once — that is what makes a fin different from everything in §04.

The fin equation

Balance the shaded slice — — with steady state, 1-D conduction, no generation, negligible radiation, uniform and constant . Substitute Fourier's law and :

General fin equation · any cross-section
This is the form your slides derive. It handles tapered, triangular and annular fins. The middle term exists only because changes with — kill it and the third term simplifies, and you get the version you will actually use.

Now specialise: uniform cross-section, so const () and (). Define the excess temperature , which turns the non-homogeneous equation into a homogeneous one:

Fin equation · uniform cross-section
P = perimeter exposed to the fluid  ·  Ac = conduction cross-sectional area  ·  m has units 1/m, so is dimensionless. For a thin rectangular fin , , giving . For a pin fin of diameter , . Use the form — it makes the tip boundary conditions far easier to apply.
Two equivalent ways to get the fin heat rate — pick the easy one

Everything that leaves the fin entered through its base, so differentiating at the base and integrating the convection over the whole surface must give the same number. The base derivative is almost always less work; the integral is the one to use if you are ever given instead of the boundary conditions.

What mL means physically

is convection off the sides divided by conduction along the fin. Small (short, thick, high- fin) — the fin stays near , area is used efficiently. Large (long, thin, low-) — the temperature dies out early and the far end is dead weight. Past the fin delivers 99 % of what an infinite fin would; adding length beyond that is wasted metal.

Three numbers examiners love

Fin efficiency · ประสิทธิภาพครีบ
Compares the real fin to a hypothetical fin at everywhere (infinite ). Range ; as . is the fin's own wetted area.
qmax depends on the fin shape — get Af right
The factor 2 in the annular case is there because both faces of the disc convect. Forgetting it halves your answer, and it is the single most common slip in annular-fin problems.
Fin effectiveness · ประสิทธิผลของครีบ
Compares the fin to the bare base area it covers up. means the fin made things worse. means it did nothing. Rule of thumb: fins are only justified if .
Fin resistance
This is the bridge back to §04: a fin is just another resistance, and it sits in parallel with the exposed base between it and the fins beside it.
When are fins most effective? (Assignment II Q16, Q19, Q20)

From : high (copper, aluminium), large — thin, closely spaced fins — and, counter-intuitively, low . So fins go on the gas side, never the liquid side. A car radiator has fins on the air side; the water side is bare. Q20's answer: put them on the exterior, where the air is.

Fin arrays — ชุดครีบ

Real hardware has fins plus the exposed base between them. Lump both into one number:

Overall surface efficiency
is the unfinned base area still exposed. sits between and 1, because the bare base is 100 % efficient. Circuit picture: fin resistances in parallel with the exposed-base resistance, all collapsed into one .

If the fins are attached rather than integral EXAM-READY

A brazed or glued fin sits on a contact resistance right where the flux is highest. Your slides carry the corrected array formulas (Incropera Eqs. 3.104–3.105):

is the fin's base cross-section — the footprint through which its heat must pass. Perfect contact means , so and the expression collapses to the ordinary . Since always, : attaching fins can only ever hurt.

Two-dimensional steady conductionการนำความร้อนคงตัวในสองมิติ

Period 9Incropera §4.1–4.3, 4S.1Slides Chapter 4a

When the temperature depends on two coordinates, , the heat flux has two components and the resistance shortcut dies. Three ways out, in increasing order of usefulness:

Method 1 · exact

Separation of variables

Beautiful, gives an exact series. Works only for simple rectangles with simple boundary conditions. You need to be able to reproduce the derivation.

Method 2 · graphical

Flux plot / shape factor

Sketch isotherms and adiabats by hand, count squares. Crude for numbers, excellent for insight — and shape factors from a table are exam gold.

Method 3 · numerical

Finite difference

Any geometry, any boundary condition. This is what real engineering uses, and it is §09.

Separation of variables, step by step

Classic problem: a rectangular plate , . Three sides held at , the top side at . Non-dimensionalise with so the boundary values become 0, 0, 0 and 1:

  1. Assume the solution separates: . Substitute: A function of alone equals a function of alone, so both must equal a constant. That constant is the whole trick.
  2. Two ODEs: , and .
  3. Apply the three homogeneous BCs. . , so . , which forces the eigenvalues
  4. Superpose (the equation is linear, so any sum of solutions is a solution):
  5. Use the last, non-homogeneous BC and expand 1 as a Fourier sine series to extract .
The result · worth memorising the shape, not the constants
The factor is 2 for odd and 0 for even — only odd terms survive. The series converges fast: three or four terms are usually enough away from the corners.

For a square plate the exact centre value is — by symmetry, four such problems superposed give everywhere. One term already gives 0.2537; three terms give 0.2499. Isotherms and heat-flow lines always cross at right angles — that is the geometric fact the next method exploits.

Flux plotting — การวาดเส้นการไหลของความร้อน

A hand method for problems with isothermal and adiabatic boundaries. The recipe:

  1. Find every line of symmetry. A symmetry line carries no heat across it, so it is an adiabat. Use it to shrink the domain — often to a quarter or an eighth.
  2. Draw the isotherms, starting from the known isothermal boundaries.
  3. Draw the heat-flow lines (adiabats) so they meet the isotherms at 90°, and so each cell is a curvilinear square: , i.e. .
  4. Count. = number of heat-flow lanes, = number of temperature increments.
Flux plot result

CheckWhy are lines of symmetry always adiabatic?

Because a symmetry line has identical conditions mirrored on both sides, the temperature gradient across it must be zero: . By Fourier's law that means — no heat crosses. Which is precisely the definition of an insulated (adiabatic) surface.

This is not a curiosity, it is a time-saver. It let §06 turn a wall into an wall, and in flux plotting it lets you analyse one-eighth of a square channel instead of the whole thing.

Finite differences & Gauss–Seidelระเบียบวิธีผลต่างสืบเนื่อง

Periods 10–11Incropera §4.4–4.5Slides Chapter 4b

Give up on a continuous . Instead lay a grid over the body, ask only for the temperature at the nodes, and replace the PDE by algebra. Four steps, every time:

The procedure

1. Grid the domain, label nodes — counts , counts . 2. Write one equation per unknown node, using the energy balance method. 3. Assemble into and apply boundary conditions. 4. Solve by matrix inversion or by iteration.

Where the interior-node equation comes from

Route 1 — Taylor series. The second-order central difference is

Accurate to order . Substituting into with gives the result below.

Route 2 — energy balance (preferred). Draw a control volume around the node and assume all heat flows are into it. Then you never have to guess a direction, and boundary nodes are no harder than interior ones:

Interior node, Δx = Δy, no generation
In words: every interior node is the plain average of its four neighbours. That single sentence is the whole method — everything else is a variation for nodes that are missing neighbours or have a fluid on one side.
Node typeFinite-difference equation (Δx = Δy)

Interior with generation
Plane surface with convection
Exterior corner, convection
Interior corner, convection
Adiabatic / symmetry surfaceset above:
Why the 2 appears in surface-node equations

A node sitting on a surface owns only half a control volume. Two of its conduction paths carry area instead of , while the inward path keeps full area — multiply through by 2 to clear the halves and the interior neighbour picks up the factor 2. If you derive by energy balance instead of memorising, you get these coefficients right automatically. Do not memorise the table — derive the one you need.

Solving the system

Direct: . Fine for the 6–8 node systems you will meet by hand; hopeless for the millions of nodes in real CFD, because is sparse and inversion destroys the sparsity.

Iterative — Gauss–Seidel. Rearrange each equation so its own node sits alone on the left, then sweep repeatedly, immediately reusing every value you have just updated:

Gauss–Seidel
Note the superscripts: values already updated this sweep use ; values not yet reached use . Stop when for every node. Convergence is guaranteed if the matrix is diagonally dominant, — reorder the equations to make it so.

Transient conduction I — the lumped capacitance methodการนำความร้อนไม่คงตัว · วิธีความจุรวม

Period 12Incropera §5.1–5.3Slides Chapter 5a

Now . The general problem is a PDE in space and time — genuinely hard. The lumped capacitance method makes it trivial by betting that the body has no internal temperature gradient at all: only. When that bet is safe, transient conduction becomes a one-line ODE.

The derivation, all of it
The results you must know cold
The time constant is thermal resistance × thermal capacitance — the exact analogue of an RC circuit discharging. After the body has covered 63 % of its journey; after , 98 %.

When is it allowed? The Biot number — เลขบิโอต์

Compare the resistance to conduction inside the solid with the resistance to convection off its surface:

Biot number
Characteristic length : a plane wall of half-thickness gives ; a long cylinder gives ; a sphere gives .
The definition trap, and it is a real one

For checking the criterion use — so for a sphere. But for the one-term series solutions of §11, the tables are built on for cylinders and spheres, and (half-thickness) for a wall. Same symbol , two different lengths, depending on which method you are in. Write down which one you are using every single time.

Read the Biot number as a picture

: the solid conducts far better than the surface convects, so the inside is nearly isothermal and the whole temperature drop sits in the fluid film. A copper ball in air. : the surface sheds heat far faster than the interior can supply it, so a steep gradient develops inside. A brick in a water quench.

Rewriting the exponent exposes the two dimensionless groups that own the whole of Chapter 5:

Fourier number is dimensionless time. It is literally "how far the thermal signal has diffused, compared with the size of the body". So .

When the loss is by radiation instead of convection

If the sphere loses heat only by radiation to large surroundings, — no longer linear, so no clean exponential. The integral gives an implicit relation involving and terms (Incropera Eq. 5.18). Twelve questions · answer out loud, then check

No calculator needed for most of these. If you cannot answer one, the section it belongs to is where your revision time should go.

Q1Why does Fourier's law have a minus sign?

Because heat flows from hot to cold, i.e. down the temperature gradient. If , the flux in must be positive, so a minus sign is required. It is the second law wearing a disguise. → §01

Q2In a cylindrical shell at steady state with no generation, is q″ constant with r? Is q constant?

is not — it falls as because the area grows. is — energy has nowhere else to go. This is Assignment II Q1. → §05

Q3Two resistances in series, one ten times the other. Which one determines the heat rate?

The large one, almost entirely — , so removing the small one changes by only 9 %. This is why storm winds barely change a well-insulated wall's heat loss. → §04, Homework II part (d)

Q4Why can you not use a thermal resistance across a region with internal generation?

presumes a single through the element. With generation, is different at the two faces, so there is no single value to write. Integrate the heat equation instead. → §06

Q5ε_f = 0.8 for a proposed fin. Should you install it?

No — it makes things worse. means the fin removes less heat than the bare base area it covers. Its own conduction resistance outweighs the extra area. Typical when is low or is high. → §07

Q6η_f = 1.0 would mean what physically? Is it achievable?

The entire fin sits at the base temperature — infinite , or zero length. Approached but never reached; as . → §07

Q7Insulating a thin wire can make it lose MORE heat. Explain in one sentence.

Adding insulation increases the conduction resistance but also increases the outer surface area, cutting the convection resistance — and below the second effect wins. → §05

Q8Why is a line of symmetry adiabatic?

Identical conditions on both sides ⇒ zero normal gradient ⇒ zero normal flux by Fourier's law. Use it to halve or quarter every symmetric problem. → §08

Q9State the interior nodal equation in words, and say why a surface node has a factor of 2.

"Each interior node is the average of its four neighbours." A surface node owns only half a control volume, so two of its conduction paths have half the area; clearing the halves doubles the coefficient on the inward neighbour. → §09

Q10What is L_c for a sphere when checking Bi, and what is it when using Table 5.1?

for the lumped-validity check (); for the one-term series and Table 5.1. Getting these backwards is the most common Chapter 5 error. → §10, §11

Q11You get Fo = 0.09 from a one-term formula. What do you do?

Stop — the one-term approximation is not valid below . Use more terms of the series, or if is very small use the semi-infinite solid solution, which is the correct model at short times. Say this explicitly in your answer. → §11

Q12A body cools with τ = 300 s. Roughly what fraction of its excess temperature is left after 10 minutes?

, so — about 14 % remains. Memorise , , , and you can estimate these in your head. → §10
